 Has Your Sunscreen Stopped Working? Signs It’s Time To Buy A New One
 By MiNDFOOD
 October 24, 2026 
 October 24, 2026 
 Are you using an old bottle of sunscreen? You could be putting your skin at risk. Here's how to tell you should pick up a new one. Despite awareness around sun protection being crucial to protect skin from premature aging and skin cancer, a recent poll found people still aren’t regularly buying a new product.
 A survey of 30,000 people across England, Scotland and Wales, conducted by Worldpanel by Numerator for Nivea Sun, found that only 56% reported that they had purchased sunscreen within the past two years.
 It can be tempting to simply dig out an old bottle of sunscreen from the back of the cupboard rather than heading out to buy a new one – but can you still rely on it to provide the same level of protection?
 We spoke to Dr Ross Perry, skin cancer expert and medical director of Cosmedics, who highlighted seven red flags to look out for when it comes to your sunscreen and explained when it should be replaced.
 Expired expiry date
 Pay attention to the expiry date.
 “With time things do degrade, so if there’s an expiry date on your sunscreen, that’s definitely something to look at,” advises Perry. “If the expiry date has passed, replace it.”
 Changes in texture
 “Sometimes sunscreen can become very thick, hard and clumped inside the tube, and doesn’t rub into the skin as well as you would expect it to, or sometimes it can actually go the other way and become very watery and start separating,” says Perry.
 “If you experience either of those situations, then get a new sunblock.”
 Left in hot or damp environments
 It’s also important to think about how your sunscreen has been stored.
 “Sunscreens aren’t bulletproof to environmental factors such as heat. So, if it has been stored in strong sunlight or has been left in a cold, damp place, that will probably have an effect on the actual physical constituents of the product,” says Perry.
 Opened for a long time
 “Once sunscreen has been opened it will degrade over a period time, because once air gets into a product, it will have an impact on it,” says Perry.
 Signs of mould
 “If there’s any darkness on the lid of the bottle or tube of sunscreen or around the edge of the opening, that can often indicate that there’s mould there – and that certainly would be a reason to discard it,” says the doctor.
 Skin irritation
 “If you use a sunscreen outside of its expiry date or don’t store it properly or if it’s been open for a long time, then the constituents of the product will degrade to a degree and might cause some irritation to your skin,” explains Perry.
 Recurring sunburn
 “Another red flag is if you’re finding that you’re burning, despite applying your sunscreen correctly,” notes Perry. “That could suggest you’re not applying enough, not reapplying frequently enough, or that the product isn’t providing the level of protection you need.”
 How often should we replace sunscreen?
 “I think replacing your sunscreen every year is a good rule of thumb,” recommends Perry. “But if you have a sunscreen in the cupboard and haven’t opened it yet, then just look at the expiry date.”
 What should we look for in a new sunscreen?
 Firstly, decide what you want to use it for.
 “If you want a product for day-to-day use, then there’s sunblock in some make-up and moisturisers which can be effective, but it really depends on how much time you’re going to be spending out in the sun,” says Perry.
 The problem with many tinted SPF products is that many people don’t apply enough to achieve the protection listed on the bottle.
 “If you’re in the office or are indoors all day, then having a thick, heavy sunscreen is probably not necessary. However, if you are outdoors in the afternoons or during the weekends, then you probably want a dedicated sunblock.”
 Perry recommends choosing a broad-spectrum SPF30 or 50 and applying it generously and reapplying regularly, particularly after swimming, sweating or towelling yourself dry.
 “I would recommend having a separate sunscreen for holidays because you want something you can use liberally, particularly if you’re sweating or going in and out of pools,” he suggests.
 “If you’re fair-skinned, you ideally want to be using a factor 50 sunscreen. However, if you’re more olive-skinned, then you can probably get away with a factor 30.”
 The doctor also reinforces the importance of storing it properly.
 “Store your sunscreen at room temperature. For example, somewhere like your bathroom cabinet where it’s out of strong sunlight and won’t get too much variation in temperature,” advises Perry.
